stages.name: Link one object and run it
hints: Read the 64-byte ELF header, then the section header table it points at, and keep the SHF_ALLOC sections
Give .text an address, write one PT_LOAD segment that covers it, and set e_entry to the address of _start
e_type is ET_EXEC (2), e_machine EM_X86_64 (62); the output has to be chmod 0755 or the kernel will not run it
Nothing here needs relocation yet: one object with no .rela sections is the whole job

tests.name: a one-object program links
the linked program runs and prints
the exit status is the one the code asked for
the output is an ET_EXEC x86-64 executable
the output is marked executable
the output satisfies every layout invariant
a second link of the same object behaves the same
an object with no .rodata at all still links

stages.name: Reject what is not an x86-64 relocatable object
hints: Check e_ident first — the four magic bytes, EI_CLASS 2 (ELFCLASS64), EI_DATA 1 (little-endian) — then e_type ET_REL and e_machine EM_X86_64, and refuse anything else before reading a single section header
A refusal is an exit status, not a panic: write one line to stderr that names the offending input file, exit non-zero, and leave no runnable output behind
An executable and a shared object are ELF too, and a static linker that only understands relocatable objects has to say so rather than folding their headers into its own output
Validate every input before allocating anything, so that a bad third input does not leave a half-written executable in place of the old one

tests.name: a good relocatable object still links and runs
a file whose ELF magic is wrong is refused
an ELFCLASS32 object is refused
a big-endian object is refused
an i386 object is refused
an aarch64 object is refused
an ET_EXEC input is refused
an ET_DYN input is not linked in as if it were a relocatable object
a foreign input is refused even when a good object comes first

stages.name: Read the ELF header of an input
hints: Take e_shoff, e_shentsize and e_shnum out of the header and walk the section header table from there: the table is wherever e_shoff says, not at a fixed offset such as 0x40
EI_OSABI, EI_ABIVERSION, the seven reserved e_ident padding bytes and e_flags are all information an x86-64 static linker ignores; refusing them means refusing real compiler output
A relocatable object's e_entry and e_phoff are meaningless — the executable's entry comes from the entry symbol you resolve, and its program headers are ones you write yourself
The table is exactly e_shnum entries of e_shentsize bytes; whatever follows it in the file is not yours to read

tests.name: the section header table is found through e_shoff, wherever it sits
e_shnum bounds the walk: bytes after the table are never read
a GNU/Linux EI_OSABI and a non-zero EI_ABIVERSION are still linkable
a non-zero e_flags is not a reason to refuse
a relocatable object's e_entry never becomes the executable's entry
a relocatable object has no program headers and the executable gets its own
the reserved e_ident padding bytes are ignored
an object with every ignorable header field set at once still runs

stages.name: String tables: section and symbol names
hints: Section names come out of the string table e_shstrndx points at; symbol names come out of the one .symtab's sh_link points at — two tables, two indices, and neither is guaranteed to be the last section
A name is the NUL-terminated string at its offset: read to the NUL, never to a fixed maximum, and keep the whole thing
Compare whole names and nothing less: `strings` is a suffix of `.rodata.strings` and `counter` is a suffix of `mycounter`, and they are four different names
Assembler and compiler output is full of dots, dollars and digits in symbol names; a name is bytes, not an identifier

tests.name: a 66-character section name survives the link and its code runs
a 131-character symbol name resolves across two objects
an undefined symbol with a 131-character name is named in full
symbol names containing dots, dollars, underscores and digits resolve
two sections whose names share a suffix stay distinct
a symbol whose name is a suffix of another's is not confused with it
section names are found through e_shstrndx, not at a fixed index
long, punctuated and suffix-sharing names in one object still print

stages.name: A section header table that lies
hints: Bounds-check before you dereference: e_shoff + e_shnum * e_shentsize must fit in the file, and so must sh_offset + sh_size of every section that occupies file space
An ELF64 section header is exactly 64 bytes, so an e_shentsize that says anything else means this is not a file you can read
Check that .symtab's sh_link is in range and really names a SHT_STRTAB before reading any symbol name through it
Refusing is right and tolerating can be right, but crashing, hanging and silently writing a broken executable never are

tests.name: an e_shoff past the end of the file is refused
an absurd e_shnum is refused
a section whose sh_offset is past the end of the file is refused
a section whose sh_size is absurd is refused
an e_shentsize of 32 is refused
an e_shstrndx out of range is never silently accepted
a .symtab whose sh_link is not a string table is refused
a .symtab whose sh_link is out of range is refused

stages.name: Truncated and malformed objects
hints: Read the whole input into memory once and check every offset and length against that buffer before using it — a truncated object is exactly a file whose offsets point past its end
The three places a truncation shows up are the 64-byte header, the section contents and the section header table; a bounds check in one of the three is a bounds check in none of them
Refusing has to be an exit status with a message on stderr, not an index panic and not a silent zero-filled read
If you have already created the output file when you discover the problem, remove it or never mark it executable: a failed link must not leave something runnable behind

tests.name: an object cut short inside the ELF header is refused
an object cut to exactly 64 bytes is refused
an object cut inside its section contents is refused
an object cut inside the section header table is refused
an object one byte short of complete is refused
an empty file never becomes a runnable program
a truncated object next to a good one still fails the link
many truncation lengths, none crashing, hanging or leaving a binary

stages.name: Odd but legal objects
hints: A section type you do not recognise is not an error: if it is not SHF_ALLOC it contributes nothing to the image, so skip it and say nothing
Nothing says .rela.text comes after .text, or that .symtab is last: index the section header table by number, never walk it expecting an order
sh_addralign 0 and 1 both mean 'no constraint', and an empty SHF_ALLOC section is legal — give it an address and move on
An input that contributes no bytes at all still contributes its symbols, and an input with no symbols at all is still a legal object

tests.name: an object with nothing but a symbol table links beside a real one
an unknown OS-specific section type that is not SHF_ALLOC is ignored
.rela.text emitted before .text still relocates correctly
non-allocatable .comment and .note sections are ignored
a section with sh_addralign 0 is treated as 1
an empty .text in one object with the real code in another links and runs
an object with no section symbols at all links and runs
a relocatable object whose .text carries a non-zero sh_addr is relocated

stages.name: The ELF header of the executable
hints: Write `e_type = ET_EXEC` (2), not `ET_DYN`: this track links non-PIE static executables, so the addresses in the file are the addresses the program runs at
`e_ehsize` is 64, `e_phentsize` 56 and `e_shentsize` 64 — these are structure sizes, not choices, and a kernel that disagrees with them refuses the file
`e_ident[7..16]` is padding and must be zero, `e_version` and `e_ident[6]` are both 1, and `e_flags` is 0 on x86-64 — there are no processor flags to set
Emit a `.symtab` (and its `.strtab`) naming the globals you defined: the suite looks `_start` up there, and so does every debugger and every `nm`

tests.name: the output is an ET_EXEC ELFCLASS64 little-endian x86-64 file
e_version is 1 and the e_ident padding is zero
e_ehsize, e_phentsize and e_shentsize are the ELF64 structure sizes
e_phoff points past the header at a table of at least one entry
e_entry is not zero and the program starts there
e_flags is zero — x86-64 defines no processor flags
the output carries a .symtab naming the globals it defined
the same header invariants hold for a program with .data and .bss

stages.name: Program headers and PT_LOAD
hints: The kernel maps `PT_LOAD` segments and ignores section headers entirely, so every allocated section has to end up inside one of them
Group the output sections by permission and emit one `PT_LOAD` per group; one segment per section also works, it is just wasteful of pages
`p_filesz` is what is read from the file and `p_memsz` what is mapped, so `p_filesz <= p_memsz` always, and the difference is `.bss`
This is a static link: no `PT_INTERP` and no `PT_DYNAMIC`, because there is no loader to name and nothing for it to do

tests.name: the output has at least one PT_LOAD and satisfies every layout invariant
p_filesz never exceeds p_memsz
no two PT_LOAD segments cover the same address
every allocated section of the output lies inside some PT_LOAD
a static link has no PT_INTERP and no PT_DYNAMIC
the program header table itself lies inside the file
the entry point lies inside an executable PT_LOAD
no PT_LOAD is mapped at address zero

stages.name: The entry point
hints: `e_entry` is `symbol_address("_start")` after resolution — look it up, never assume it is the base of `.text` or the first byte of the first input
`_start` can live in any input, at any offset in any section, with other symbols in front of it; the address is section base plus `st_value`
`-e name` replaces the symbol that is looked up, and nothing else: the layout, the sections and every other address stay exactly as they were
The kernel jumps straight to `e_entry` with no return address on the stack, so `_start` must never `ret` — it exits with a syscall

tests.name: e_entry is the address _start has in the output's own symbol table
the bytes at e_entry are the input's first .text bytes
the entry point sits in an executable segment
_start in the second object is still found
_start at a non-zero offset in its section is found
a symbol defined before _start does not become the entry point
-e names a different entry symbol
the program really begins at e_entry

stages.name: Segment permissions and W^X
hints: Turn `SHF_EXECINSTR` into `PF_X` and `SHF_WRITE` into `PF_W`, always keeping `PF_R`: a segment nothing can read is a segment nothing can use
Group sections by the permission set they end up with and give each group its own `PT_LOAD`, so that `.text` never shares a segment with `.data`
No `PT_LOAD` may carry both `PF_W` and `PF_X` — merging read-only data into the text segment is fine, merging `.data` into it is not
Permissions are enforced by the MMU at page granularity, so two sections that share a page share its permissions whatever the section headers say

tests.name: the segment holding .text is executable
the segment holding .data is writable
no PT_LOAD is both writable and executable
a program that stores to .data and reads it back works
the segment holding .rodata is readable
a program that writes to .bss and reads it back works
code contributed by a second object is executable too
the permissions hold for a program with .text, .rodata, .data and .bss

stages.name: Page alignment and the mmap congruence
hints: For every `PT_LOAD`, `p_offset % 0x1000` must equal `p_vaddr % 0x1000`; the easy way to guarantee it is to start each segment on a page boundary in both
`p_align` is the alignment the segment was laid out for: a power of two, and at least the page size for anything the kernel maps
Rounding the address up to a page and the offset up to a page independently is the classic bug — round one of them and then derive the other
A section whose `sh_addralign` is larger than a page (a 64 KiB table, say) raises the segment's `p_align` too, and the congruence still has to hold

tests.name: every PT_LOAD has p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo the page size
every PT_LOAD's p_align is a power of two and at least a page
the kernel runs the result, which is the real judge
a .rodata that spills onto a second page still runs with its bytes intact
a section aligned to 64 KiB keeps the congruence
the loadable segments come out in increasing address order
a program with .text, .rodata, .data and .bss is congruent everywhere
every segment's file range lies inside the file

stages.name: .bss: memory without file bytes
hints: An `SHT_NOBITS` input section has a size but no bytes: advance the output address by its size and copy nothing, because `sh_offset` points at other sections' data
The segment that covers `.bss` gets `p_memsz` larger than `p_filesz`; the difference is what the kernel zero-fills, and it is the whole trick
Put every `SHT_NOBITS` section last inside its segment — file bytes have to be contiguous from `p_offset`, so nothing with real bytes may follow the hole
`.bss` must land in a writable, non-executable segment, and a megabyte of it must not add a megabyte to the output file

tests.name: .bss comes out of the linker as SHT_NOBITS
.bss occupies no bytes in the output file
the PT_LOAD covering .bss has p_memsz larger than p_filesz
the .bss bytes are zero at run time
a program writes to .bss and reads it back
.bss from two objects is allocated for both
a one-megabyte .bss does not make the output a megabyte bigger
.bss is not inside a read-only segment

stages.name: Concatenating input sections
hints: Collect the input sections by output name, then place them one after another, remembering for each contribution the offset it was given
Keep the command-line order: every linker lays contributions down in the order the inputs were named, and programs — and debuggers — rely on it
Round the running address up to each contribution's own `sh_addralign` before placing it, not once for the whole output section
A symbol's output address is the address its contribution got plus its input `st_value`; get this wrong by one contribution and every relocation is wrong

tests.name: .text from three objects is concatenated and all of it runs
.rodata from three objects is all present and each string is intact
input sections come out in command-line order
reversing the command line reverses the addresses
each contribution keeps its own sh_addralign
a symbol inside a contribution keeps its offset within it
.data from three objects is concatenated and the program reads all of it
each contribution's bytes survive concatenation unchanged

stages.name: Alignment and empty sections
hints: Round the running address up with `(addr + align - 1) & !(align - 1)`, and treat an `sh_addralign` of 0 or 1 as no constraint rather than as a divisor
A zero-size section contributes nothing: do not let it advance the address, and do not let it create an output section out of nothing
An alignment larger than a page raises the segment's `p_align`, and the page congruence still has to hold — pad the file to match, or pick the offset from the address
Symbols in an empty section are legal; they just all have the same address, and they must not end up pointing outside every segment

tests.name: sections aligned to 16, 64, 256, 4096 and 65536 bytes all land aligned
an sh_addralign of 0 is treated as 1
an empty .text in one object does not break the link
a zero-size .rodata is harmless
alignment is respected when several objects contribute the same section
a 64 KiB alignment does not break the page congruence
an object that contributes nothing but an empty section still links
the padding between two aligned contributions corrupts neither

stages.name: A global defined in another object
hints: Make one pass over every input first, recording each STB_GLOBAL definition (name, its object, its section and st_value) before you try to patch anything
A relocation's S is the *output* address of the symbol it names: the address the defining input section was given, plus the symbol's st_value inside it
Undefined entries (st_shndx == SHN_UNDEF) are references, not definitions — an object mentioning a name never means it provides it
Command-line order must not change the answer here: with only objects on the line, every one of them is loaded, so `a.o b.o` and `b.o a.o` link the same program

tests.name: a call to a global defined in another object links and runs
the call displacement is S + A - P for the addresses the linker chose
a chain of three objects resolves
a data symbol defined in another object is read at run time
the resolved callee lies inside an executable segment
the resolved symbol appears in the output's .symtab as a definition
the same two objects in the other order link the same program
two objects referring to the same global get the same address

stages.name: An undefined symbol is an error
hints: After collecting every definition, walk every relocation: if the symbol it names is still SHN_UNDEF and not weak, that is an error, not a zero
The message has to contain the symbol's name — a learner debugging a 200-object link needs the name far more than they need your wording
Report every unresolved name you find, not just the first, and exit non-zero
Delete (or never create) the output file on failure: a stale a.out that a build system thinks is fresh is worse than no output at all

tests.name: an undefined function symbol names the symbol in the diagnostic
an undefined data symbol names the symbol in the diagnostic
the failing link exits non-zero
a failed link leaves no runnable output behind
two undefined symbols are both reported
an undefined symbol referenced from .data is an error too
a reference another object satisfies is not an error
an undefined weak symbol is not an error at all

stages.name: A duplicate definition is an error
hints: Keep one table keyed by name; inserting a strong definition where a strong definition already sits is the error, and the message must carry the name
Only *definitions* collide — an SHN_UNDEF entry for the same name is a reference and must never trip the check
A strong definition and a weak one are legal: the strong one wins silently, and a second weak one is not an error either
The same file named twice on the command line is two inputs, not one; do not deduplicate by path to make the error go away

tests.name: two strong definitions of one function name the symbol
two strong definitions of one datum name the symbol
the same object passed twice is an error
a definition in .text and another in .data still collide
a duplicate nothing references is still an error
the failing link exits non-zero and leaves no runnable output
a definition plus a reference is not a duplicate
a strong definition beside a weak one is legal and the strong one wins

stages.name: Local symbols do not clash
hints: Resolve a relocation against a local symbol inside the object that owns it: take the symbol index straight out of that object's own .symtab and never consult the global table
The binding half of st_info decides everything; sh_info of .symtab tells you where the locals stop, and locals always come first
A local never enters the global table, so two objects may each have a local `helper` and a third object's reference to `helper` must still find the global one — or fail as undefined if there is none
Section symbols (STT_SECTION, empty name) are locals too: `.rodata` in five objects means five distinct section symbols with five distinct addresses

tests.name: two objects with a local of the same name each use their own
changing a local's value changes only its own object's answer
a local is invisible outside its object, so a global of that name wins
a reference to a name that is only ever local is undefined
section symbols of identically named sections do not clash
locals link cleanly where the same names as globals would collide
the control program still satisfies every layout invariant

stages.name: Weak definitions and weak references
hints: A strong definition always beats a weak one, whichever input it came from and in whatever order the objects are named — the winner must not depend on the command line
A weak definition is still a definition: with no strong one in the link it is used, and it never counts as a duplicate
An unresolved weak *reference* is not an error; compute the relocation with S = 0 and let the program test for it
Two weak definitions of one name are not an error either; pick one deterministically (GNU ld takes the first it sees) and move on

tests.name: a strong definition beats a weak one
a weak definition is used when it is the only one
two weak definitions resolve to one of the two
an unresolved weak reference is zero and the code can branch on it
a weak data symbol is used like any other
the strong definition wins in either command-line order
a weak reference a strong definition satisfies is not zero
every weak combination links without an error

stages.name: Common symbols (SHN_COMMON)
hints: For a symbol whose st_shndx is SHN_COMMON, st_value is the required alignment and st_size the required size — neither means what it means for a normal symbol
Merge every common of one name into a single .bss allocation whose size is the largest st_size and whose alignment is the largest st_value, then give every reference that one address
Commons never collide with each other, but any real definition — .data, .bss, .text, strong or weak — takes precedence and the commons are dropped
The allocation is zero-filled and writable: it belongs in a SHT_NOBITS section inside a read-write PT_LOAD, and costs no bytes in the file

tests.name: a single common symbol is allocated once, zeroed, in .bss
two commons of different sizes get the largest size
two commons of different alignments get the largest alignment
a real definition beats a common and is not an error
the same common in three objects is not a duplicate definition
a common symbol is writable at run time
two objects referring to one common share the one allocation

stages.name: Visibility, absolute and section symbols
hints: st_other's low two bits are the visibility; in a static link with no dynamic table they change nothing about resolution, so read them, keep them, and never refuse a link over them
A symbol whose st_shndx is SHN_ABS already has its final value: S is st_value itself, with no section address added — this is the one case where relocating is the bug
A relocation may name a STT_SECTION symbol instead of a real one; S is then the output address the section was given, and the addend picks the byte inside it
STT_FILE entries are local, absolute and carry a source file name; skip them rather than treating them as definitions of anything

tests.name: an STV_HIDDEN global still resolves inside the link
an STV_INTERNAL global still resolves inside the link
an SHN_ABS symbol keeps its exact value through the link
a relocation against an SHN_ABS symbol produces that exact value
a section symbol is usable as a relocation target
an STT_FILE symbol is ignored rather than rejected
st_size and st_info of a defined global survive into the output
visibility does not change the address anything resolves to

stages.name: The entry symbol and -e
hints: Resolve the entry name through the same global symbol table as everything else, then put its final address — section address plus st_value — in e_entry
`-e name` and `--entry=name` are the same option; with neither, the name is `_start`, and it may be defined in any input, not just the first
The entry symbol need not sit at offset 0 of its section: st_value is part of the answer and dropping it points e_entry at whatever happens to be first
Decide what to do when the entry name is undefined and say so — GNU ld warns and carries on with a defaulted address, which is friendly but easy to miss; failing outright is also defensible

tests.name: with no -e the entry point is _start
-e names another entry point
--entry= is the same option in its long spelling
the program really starts at the chosen entry
an entry symbol away from offset 0 keeps its st_value
the entry symbol may be defined in the second object
a missing _start is diagnosed
an -e naming nothing is diagnosed

stages.name: R_X86_64_PC32 and R_X86_64_PLT32
hints: Walk every SHT_RELA section of every input and compute S + A - P for each entry: S is the final address of the symbol, A is r_addend, P is the final address of the four-byte field being patched

P is the address of the field, not of the instruction — the -4 the assembler already folded into the addend is what turns that into the end of the instruction the processor measures displacements from

Treat R_X86_64_PLT32 exactly like R_X86_64_PC32: with no PLT to build, a static link resolves both straight to the symbol, and a linker that handles only one of them dies on the first real compiler output it sees
Write the result into the output image as a little-endian signed 32-bit value, never back into the input object, and check that it fits before storing it

tests.name: a cross-object call is patched to S + A - P
the same call encoded as R_X86_64_PC32 behaves identically
a lea reaches a string in .rodata
a backward reference gets a negative displacement
two relocations in one section are both patched
a relocation living in the second object is patched too
a jmp reaches a label in another object
a PC32 against a symbol nothing defines names the symbol

stages.name: R_X86_64_64
hints: R_X86_64_64 is the easy one: store the 64-bit value S + A, little-endian, into the eight bytes at the relocation's site — no program counter, no truncation, no range check
The site is in a data section, not in .text, so the patch loop has to run over every relocated section of every input and not just over the code
Patch the bytes of the output image after the section has been copied into it: patching the input object's buffer and copying afterwards works only until two inputs share a section name
A relocation inside .rodata is still applied — read-only is a property of the final mapping, not a reason to leave the word zero

tests.name: a .data pointer to .rodata is loaded and used at run time
the eight bytes hold S + A and nothing around them moves
an array of three pointers is patched entry by entry
a pointer with a non-zero addend points into the middle of the object
a pointer to a symbol defined in another object
an R_X86_64_64 inside .rodata is relocated too
a pointer to a function holds that function's address
an R_X86_64_64 against a symbol nothing defines names the symbol

stages.name: R_X86_64_32 and R_X86_64_32S
hints: Both kinds compute S + A and store the low 32 bits; the only difference is the range they are allowed to hold, so share the arithmetic and split only the check
These are the relocations that make the small code model work: the whole image is below 4 GB, so a zero-extended 32-bit immediate is a complete pointer and the program can dereference it as one
An R_X86_64_32 can sit in a data section as easily as in an instruction — a four-byte word holding an address is the same relocation as `mov eax, $sym`
Do not sign-extend an R_X86_64_32 or zero-extend an R_X86_64_32S when checking the range: 0xffffffff is legal for the first and out of range for the second

tests.name: an R_X86_64_32 immediate holds the symbol's address
an R_X86_64_32S immediate holds the same value
both kinds in one object are patched independently
an addend shifts an R_X86_64_32 immediate
an addend shifts an R_X86_64_32S immediate
an R_X86_64_32 against a section symbol
a four-byte word in .data is a usable pointer at run time
an R_X86_64_32S resolved from another object

stages.name: Relocation overflow is a hard error
hints: After computing the value of a relocation, check it fits the field before you store it: R_X86_64_32 needs 0 <= v <= 0xffffffff, R_X86_64_32S and R_X86_64_PC32 need -0x80000000 <= v <= 0x7fffffff
The check is on S + A, not on S: an addend can carry a perfectly ordinary symbol past the end of the range
Run the check over every relocated section, data included — an overflowing pointer word in .data is as fatal as one in .text
Refusing means exiting non-zero with the symbol's name on stderr and leaving no output file behind; a truncated value produces a binary that fails far from the mistake

tests.name: an R_X86_64_32 against an absolute symbol above 4 GB is refused
an R_X86_64_32 against 0xffffffff is accepted and stored whole
an R_X86_64_32S against 0x80000000 is refused
an R_X86_64_32S against 0x7fffffff is accepted
an R_X86_64_32S reaches the bottom of its signed range
an addend that carries a legal symbol out of range is refused
a PC32 displacement that does not fit 32 bits is refused
an overflow inside .data is caught as well

stages.name: Addends, positive and negative
hints: r_addend is a signed 64-bit field of the relocation entry: read it as an i64, add it to S, and never look at what the field being patched already holds
In a SHT_RELA object the contents of the field are irrelevant — the assembler usually leaves zeros there, but a linker that adds to them instead of storing over them is only right by accident
The -4 on every RIP-relative relocation is an addend like any other; there is no special case for it, and adding a second -4 of your own doubles it
An addend may point outside the symbol it names — one past the end is normal and must not be rejected

tests.name: a positive addend prints from the middle of a string
a negative addend walks back to the start of a string
an addend moves an R_X86_64_64 pointer
a large addend reaches across a big section
an addend against a section symbol is the offset into the section
an addend may land exactly on the end of a symbol
a zero addend is the plain address
the addend comes from the relocation, not from the field

stages.name: Relocations against section symbols
hints: An STT_SECTION symbol's value is the address of that object's contribution to the output section, so resolve it to where you placed that input section — not to the start of the merged output section
The offset inside the section is carried entirely in r_addend, which is why these relocations almost always have a large addend and no name

Two inputs both contributing .rodata have two different section symbols with the same name; keying anything on the section's name instead of on the input section is how the second object's literals end up pointing into the first
A section symbol usually has an empty st_name, so a symbol table keyed by name needs somewhere else to put them

tests.name: an anonymous literal is reached through the .rodata section symbol
several literals at different offsets of one section
a zero addend on a section symbol is the start of the section
a section symbol of .data
an R_X86_64_64 against a section symbol
a PC32 against the .text section symbol reaches a function
two objects each have their own .rodata section symbol
a section symbol and a named symbol reach the same byte

stages.name: References across sections and objects
hints: Give every input section its final address before applying a single relocation: the value of a symbol is its section's address plus st_value, and that is only knowable once layout is finished
Keep one map from (input object, section index) to the address that section landed at — it answers both 'where is this symbol' and 'where is this relocation site'
A relocation's site is in the section that owns the .rela, and its target can be in any section of any object; nothing about the arithmetic changes with the direction
Data can point at code and code at data: a function pointer in .data is an R_X86_64_64 whose symbol happens to be STT_FUNC, and nothing special is needed for it

tests.name: .text reaches a string in .rodata
.text reaches a string in .data
.data holds a pointer into .text
.rodata holds a pointer into .rodata
two objects reference each other in both directions
a chain of three objects each calling the next
a section holding a pointer into itself
one program whose sections all point at each other

stages.name: GOTPCREL and its relaxation
hints: The simple implementation is a real GOT: collect every symbol a GOTPCREL names, give each one an eight-byte slot in a section you allocate, fill the slot with S, and resolve the relocation to GOT_slot + A - P
The other implementation is relaxation: in a static link S is a constant, so `mov r64, [rip+GOT]` can become `lea r64, [rip+sym]` — same length, one fewer memory reference, no GOT
Whichever road you take, the register must end up holding the address of the symbol and not the contents of it; a GOT slot holds an address, so the load reads a pointer, not the object
Only relax when you are sure: R_X86_64_GOTPCRELX and R_X86_64_REX_GOTPCRELX exist precisely to tell the linker the instruction is safe to rewrite

tests.name: a GOTPCREL load produces a usable address at run time
the linker either builds a GOT entry or relaxes the load
R_X86_64_REX_GOTPCRELX takes the same road or a shorter one
two references to the same symbol agree
a GOT reference to a function can be called through
a GOT reference to a symbol defined in another object
a GOT load and a lea of the same symbol agree at run time
a GOT reference to an undefined symbol names the symbol

stages.name: An archive on the command line
hints: Recognise an archive by its first eight bytes, `!<arch>\n`, not by the `.a` on the file name — the name is a convention and `-l` will hand you paths you did not choose

A member header is 60 bytes of space-padded ASCII; the only two fields you need are the 16-byte name and the decimal size at offset 48, and every member starts on an even offset, so round the size up when you step to the next one
A name of `/<decimal>` is an offset into the `//` member, and a short name is written with a trailing `/` that is not part of the name — strip it
Once you have a member's bytes you are back in stage 01: it is an ordinary ET_REL object and the reader you already have parses it unchanged

tests.name: a one-member archive resolves an undefined symbol
an archive supplies two members that are both needed
an archive named by a relative path is found
a member name too long for the header is read from the long-name table
an archive links beside plain objects
an archive nothing needs is not an error
one member defining both a function and a datum supplies both
an archive with no members at all is not an error
the archive's container bytes never reach the output

stages.name: Only the members that are needed
hints: Keep the set of still-undefined symbols as you go; when you reach an archive, load exactly the members that define one of them and nothing else

Loading a member adds its own undefined symbols to that set, so loop over the archive until a whole pass pulls nothing in — one pass is not enough when a member needs a member that sits earlier in the same file
A symbol that is already defined does not make a member needed, and neither does an undefined *weak* reference: a weak reference resolves to zero rather than dragging a definition in
Never validate a member you did not load — its duplicate symbols and its undefined references are somebody else's problem until the day it is needed

tests.name: a duplicate symbol inside an unused member is not a duplicate definition
an unused member's own undefined symbol is not an error
a member already defined elsewhere is never pulled in
a member is pulled in transitively by another member's reference
a member earlier in the archive is still found on a second pass
a member is pulled in for a data symbol
an undefined weak reference does not pull a member in
a member needed for two symbols is pulled in only once
the pulled members' symbols are in the output and the unused ones are not

stages.name: Order on the command line is semantics
hints: Walk the inputs strictly left to right and keep one set of still-undefined symbols; an archive reached before the reference that needs it simply has nothing to offer and is dropped
Do not go back: once an archive has been scanned and taken nothing, a reference made by a later input does not reopen it — `--start-group` is the opt-in for that, and it is stage 36
Two definitions of one symbol in two archives is not an error: the first archive on the command line supplies it and the second is simply never asked
Objects are concatenated in command-line order, so the first object's .text is the one that gets the lowest address — sorting inputs by name or by size changes every address in the output

tests.name: an archive before the object that needs it resolves nothing
the same archive after the object works
a reference made after the archive has gone past is not resolved

the same two archives in the wrong order do not
a symbol defined in two archives is taken from the first one
the same archive listed twice is not an error

the order of the objects is the order their sections are concatenated in

stages.name: -L and -l
hints: `-l <name>` means `lib<name>.a`, matched exactly — `libxy.a` is not a match for `-l x`, and the file name is built by wrapping the name, never by searching for it
Search the `-L` directories in the order they were given and take the first directory that has the file, not the last and not the best
When nothing matches, exit non-zero with a message that contains the library's name; `cannot find -lfoo` is the wording GNU ld uses and the name is the part that matters
Resolving `-l` to a path is all this option does: the archive it found is linked at the position the `-l` occupied, under the ordering rules of stage 34

tests.name: -L dir -l x finds libx.a in that directory

stages.name: Groups and broken symbol indexes
hints: `--start-group`/`--end-group` bracket a set of archives that is rescanned as a whole until a pass pulls nothing in; the loop must terminate on the first barren pass, not on a fixed number of tries
Treat the `/` index as a hint you verify, not as the truth: after opening the member it points at, check that the member really does define the symbol before you count it as resolved
An archive with no `/` member at all is still a perfectly good archive — read each member's own symbol table instead
Every malformed archive here has to end in a diagnostic and a non-zero exit, never a panic, an infinite loop or a half-written output file

tests.name: two archives with a circular dependency do not link on their own

stages.name: A six-object freestanding program
hints: Read every input before resolving anything: object six defines what object one referenced, and object one is read first
Concatenate the same-named sections in command-line order, then give each symbol its final address as output section base + input contribution offset + st_value
Apply relocations only once every address is fixed — a PLT32 call between two objects is just S + A - P as soon as both .text contributions have landed
The binary inherits argv and stdin from whoever runs it; a correct link touches neither, so the same program must behave identically however it is invoked

tests.name: a six-object program links

the exit status is the sum every object contributed

stages.name: Two hundred objects
hints: Put every global in one hash map keyed by name as the inputs are read, so resolution is one lookup per reference rather than a scan over every object
Concatenate each output section once, in input order, and remember every input contribution's base address — recomputing it per relocation is the quadratic trap
Two hundred inputs means two hundred open files; read each one once into memory and close it, or the link dies on the file-descriptor limit long before it dies on time

tests.name: two hundred objects link into one program
the program prints every line and exits with the sum
all two hundred contributions have their own address
the two hundred .text sections come out as one
two hundred objects in reverse order still link
a seeded shuffle of the command line changes nothing
a two-hundred-object link finishes inside the deadline
every layout invariant survives two hundred inputs
no symbol is left undefined after two hundred cross-references

stages.name: A five-megabyte .rodata
hints: Keep every offset, address and size in a u64 and do the arithmetic with checked or saturating operations — five megabytes is where a u32 section offset first hurts
p_filesz and p_memsz are different numbers: a SHT_NOBITS section adds to the second and never to the first, so an eight-megabyte .bss must cost zero bytes on disk
The page congruence p_offset = p_vaddr (mod 4096) has to hold for a five-megabyte segment exactly as it does for a forty-byte one; pad the file, do not move the address
Honour every input section's sh_addralign when you concatenate, including the one whose contribution ends at an odd offset — the next section starts at the next multiple, not the next byte

tests.name: a five-megabyte .rodata links

the output file is at least five megabytes
an eight-megabyte .bss adds no bytes to the file
an eight-megabyte .bss is mapped and zeroed
a five-megabyte segment still satisfies the page congruence
two hundred sixteen-kilobyte sections all land aligned
five megabytes of .rodata and eight of .bss in one program

stages.name: Fuzz: seeded mutations of valid objects
hints: Validate before you trust: every offset, size and index read out of an input has to be checked against the length of the file before it is used to slice it
Use checked arithmetic on everything that came from the file — sh_offset + sh_size overflowing a u64 is a one-line panic and a panic is a signal
Refusing an input is always allowed and accepting a harmless lie is always allowed; being killed, hanging, or exiting 0 with a broken output file never is
Never allocate a buffer of a size an input told you — sh_size can say sixteen exabytes, and the answer is a diagnostic, not a memory request

tests.name: four hundred seeded mutations never crash or hang the linker

every truncation of a valid object is handled
a corrupt section header table is never fatal to the linker

stages.name: Determinism
hints: Iterate over ordered containers only: a hash map walked in whatever order it happens to be in is the single most common source of a non-reproducible linker
Zero every byte of padding you write — an uninitialised buffer is a different output every run and a security hole in the same breath
Nothing that is not in the inputs may reach the output: not the time, not the output file's name, not the path an input was read from, not a process id
Truncate the output file when you open it; a relink over a longer previous output must not leave the old tail behind

tests.name: the same inputs linked twice are byte-identical

stages.name: readelf, nm and objdump agree
hints: If readelf prints a warning about the file, fix the field it is complaining about — it is almost always sh_link, sh_entsize or an sh_offset that runs past the end
objdump and nm read the section header table, not the program headers: an executable that runs perfectly can still be unreadable to every tool if its section headers are wrong or missing

A .symtab is optional for running and essential for debugging; emit one with st_value set to each symbol's final address, sh_link pointing at the .strtab and sh_info equal to the index of the first non-local
